prompt: In 1916, Einstein proposed three processes that occur in the formation of an atomic spectral line. Which three?

choices.text: Absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission
Absorption, fluorescence and phosphorescence
choices.why: Fluorescence and phosphorescence are kinds of emission from molecules. Einstein's three processes are absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission.

choices.text: Absorption, reflection and scattering
choices.why: Reflection and scattering don't move an electron between energy levels. Einstein's three processes are absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission.

choices.text: Spontaneous emission, internal conversion and intersystem crossing
choices.why: Internal conversion and intersystem crossing are radiationless steps in molecules. Einstein's three processes are absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission.

explanation: In absorption a photon promotes the atom to the upper level. In spontaneous emission the excited atom drops back on its own. In stimulated emission a passing photon triggers the drop.

prompt: Even with no light around, an excited atom eventually emits a photon. According to the section, what triggers this spontaneous emission?

choices.text: A perturbation from vacuum fluctuations
A passing photon of the transition frequency
choices.why: That triggers stimulated emission. Spontaneous emission needs no outside photon; the section attributes it to a perturbation from vacuum fluctuations.

choices.text: A collision with a ground-state atom
choices.why: Collisions aren't part of this picture. The trigger is a perturbation in the Hamiltonian that comes, if nothing else, from vacuum fluctuations.

choices.text: Absorption of a second, higher-energy photon
choices.why: No second photon is involved, and an excited two-level atom has no higher level to reach. The trigger is a perturbation from vacuum fluctuations.

explanation: Spontaneous emission happens without any outside influence. The section attributes its triggering to a perturbation in the Hamiltonian that comes, if nothing else, from vacuum fluctuations.

prompt: In a collection of two-level atoms, a photon with exactly the transition energy passes an atom that is already in the excited state. What can the photon do?

choices.text: Stimulate the atom to emit a second photon
Be absorbed, lifting the atom to a higher level
choices.why: A two-level atom has no higher level, so an excited atom can't absorb the photon. Instead, the photon's oscillating field can induce emission.

choices.text: Nothing, since only ground-state atoms interact with light
choices.why: Excited atoms interact with light too: the photon's time-varying field perturbs the electron at just the right frequency and can induce emission.

choices.text: Push the atom to the ground state with no photon emitted
choices.why: The atom does drop to the ground state, but it gives off a photon as it does. That is stimulated emission.

explanation: An excited two-level atom can't absorb the photon, but the photon's time-varying electromagnetic field, at just the right frequency, can induce the atom to emit. This is stimulated emission.

prompt: How does a photon produced by stimulated emission compare with the photon that stimulated it?

choices.text: Same frequency and direction, and in phase
Same frequency, but in a random direction
choices.why: The stimulated photon doesn't head off on its own: it travels in the same direction as the stimulating photon, and in phase with it.

choices.text: Twice the frequency, in the same direction
choices.why: The energy gap fixes the frequency, so the emitted photon has the same frequency as the passing one, not twice it.

choices.text: Same direction, but a lower frequency
choices.why: Both photons match the energy gap E_2 − E_1, so they have the same frequency. They also travel together and in phase.

explanation: The emitted photon has the same frequency as the passing photon, because both match the energy gap. It also moves in the same direction as the stimulating photon and in phase with it.

prompt: In stimulated emission, what happens to the photon that induces the emission?

choices.text: It continues on unchanged
It is absorbed by the excited atom
choices.why: An excited two-level atom can't absorb the photon. The stimulating photon is unaffected and continues on its way, now joined by a second photon.

choices.text: It loses half its energy to the new photon
choices.why: The new photon's energy comes from the atom's drop, E_2 − E_1, not from the passing photon, which keeps its full energy.

choices.text: It is reflected back the way it came
choices.why: The photon isn't turned around: it continues in its original direction, and the emitted photon travels alongside it.

explanation: The inducing photon is unaffected by the interaction and continues on its way. One photon goes in and two identical photons come out: the amplification in Light Amplification by the Stimulated Emission of Radiation.

prompt: A photon of the transition frequency passes two atoms, one in the ground state and one in the excited state. How does the probability that the first absorbs it compare with the probability that it stimulates emission from the second?

choices.text: The two probabilities are equal
Absorption is far more probable
choices.why: Per atom, neither result is preferred. Absorption wins in a real sample only because there are far more ground-state atoms.

choices.text: Stimulated emission is far more probable
choices.why: Per atom, the two probabilities are the same. Stimulated emission is not favored over absorption.

choices.text: Absorption is exactly twice as probable
choices.why: The section says neither result is preferred: the two probabilities are equal.

explanation: For one ground-state atom and one excited atom, absorption and stimulated emission are equally probable; neither is preferred. What tips the balance in a real sample is how many atoms are in each state.

prompt: At thermal equilibrium, the populations of a two-level atom obey N_1 = N_2 exp(ΔE/(k_B T)), where N_1 is the ground-state population, N_2 the excited-state population and ΔE > 0 the gap between them. Which state has the larger population?

choices.text: The ground state
The excited state
choices.why: With ΔE > 0 the exponential is greater than 1, so N_1 > N_2: the higher-energy state holds fewer atoms.

choices.text: Neither; they are always equal
choices.why: Equal populations would need the exponential to equal 1, which means ΔE = 0. For a real gap, N_1 > N_2.

choices.text: It depends on the temperature
choices.why: At any temperature ΔE/(k_B T) is positive, so the exponential is greater than 1 and N_1 > N_2. Temperature changes only how much larger N_1 is.

explanation: Since ΔE and k_B T are both positive, exp(ΔE/(k_B T)) is greater than 1, so N_1 > N_2. At room temperature, with ΔE ≈ 1 eV, N_1 exceeds N_2 by a factor of about e^40 = 2.4 × 10^17.

prompt: At room temperature, k_B T is about 1/40 eV. For two levels ΔE = 2.0 eV apart, what is ΔE/(k_B T)?
explanation: ΔE/(k_B T) = 2.0 eV ÷ (1/40 eV) = 2.0 × 40 = 80. So N_1/N_2 = e^80, about 5.5 × 10^34: essentially every atom is in the ground state.

prompt: At thermal equilibrium, N_1 = N_2 exp(ΔE/(k_B T)), and e = 2.718. For two levels whose gap ΔE is just equal to k_B T, what is N_1/N_2? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: With ΔE = k_B T the exponent is 1, so N_1/N_2 = e^1 = 2.718. Even for a gap as small as k_B T, the ground state holds almost three times as many atoms as the excited state.

prompt: Absorption and stimulated emission are equally likely for each atom a photon passes. Why, then, does a collection of atoms at thermal equilibrium not act as a laser?

choices.text: Far more atoms are in the ground state to absorb photons
Stimulated emission can't happen at room temperature
choices.why: Stimulated emission can happen at any temperature. The problem is numbers: ground-state atoms vastly outnumber excited ones, so photons are mostly absorbed.

choices.text: Spontaneous emission is forbidden at thermal equilibrium
choices.why: Excited atoms do emit spontaneously. Those photons are then mostly absorbed, because there are far more ground-state atoms.

choices.text: Photons pass through the atoms without interacting
choices.why: Photons do interact with the atoms. The trouble is that most of the atoms they meet are in the ground state, so absorption dominates.

explanation: At equilibrium the ground state holds vastly more atoms than the excited state, so a passing photon is much more likely to be absorbed than to stimulate emission. Spontaneously emitted photons are mostly reabsorbed, and there is no laser.

prompt: The rates of absorption and stimulated emission are proportional to the spectral radiant energy density ρ_(ν) of the light. What does ρ_(ν) measure?

choices.text: Radiant energy density per unit frequency of the light
The number of atoms per unit volume in the upper state
choices.why: That is N_2, a number density of atoms. ρ_(ν) describes the light: its radiant energy density per unit frequency.

choices.text: The probability per unit time of spontaneous emission
choices.why: That is the Einstein coefficient A_21. ρ_(ν) = dρ/dν is the radiant energy density per unit frequency.

choices.text: The energy of a single photon at the transition frequency
choices.why: One photon's energy is hν. ρ_(ν) measures how much radiant energy per unit volume the light carries per unit frequency.

explanation: ρ_(ν) = dρ/dν is the radiant energy density ρ per unit frequency of the light at the transition, in units of (J·s)/m^3. More light at the right frequency means faster absorption and stimulated emission.

prompt: The Einstein coefficient B_12 gives a probability per unit time per unit spectral energy density. A probability of which event?

choices.text: An atom in state 1 absorbing a photon
An atom in state 2 emitting a photon on its own
choices.why: That is described by A_21, in s^−1, which needs no light. B_12 is for absorption from state 1 up to state 2.

choices.text: An atom in state 2 being stimulated to emit
choices.why: That is B_21, the coefficient for stimulated emission. B_12 is for absorption from state 1 up to state 2.

choices.text: A photon passing an atom with no effect
choices.why: The Einstein coefficients describe transitions, not photons that do nothing. B_12 is the coefficient for absorption.

explanation: B_12 is the probability per unit time per unit spectral energy density that an atom in state 1 absorbs a photon of energy E_2 − E_1 = hν_12 and jumps to state 2. Multiplied by ρ_(ν)(ν_12) and N_1, it gives the absorption rate.

prompt: Each of Einstein's rates is proportional to the number of atoms in one of the two states. Which state's population sets the rate of stimulated emission?

choices.text: The upper state, N_2
The lower state, N_1
choices.why: N_1 sets the absorption rate. Stimulated emission starts from the excited state, so its rate is B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) N_2.

choices.text: The total, N_1 + N_2
choices.why: Only atoms already in the upper level can be stimulated to emit, so the rate is proportional to N_2 alone.

choices.text: The difference, N_1 − N_2
choices.why: The rate of stimulated emission itself is B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) N_2. A difference of populations appears only when it is combined with absorption.

explanation: Absorption starts from the ground state, so its rate is B_12 ρ_(ν)(ν_12) N_1. Spontaneous and stimulated emission start from the excited state, so their rates, A_21 N_2 and B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) N_2, are proportional to N_2.

prompt: The section's rate for spontaneous emission is −dN_2/dt = A_21 N_2. Why does ρ_(ν), the spectral energy density of the light, not appear in it?

choices.text: It happens without any outside influence
ρ_(ν) is always zero inside a sample of two-level atoms
choices.why: ρ_(ν) isn't zero whenever light is present; it appears in the absorption and stimulated emission rates. Spontaneous emission simply doesn't need the light.

choices.text: A_21 already includes ρ_(ν) as a hidden factor
choices.why: A_21 is a constant of the transition, a probability per unit time in s^−1. The B coefficients are the ones multiplied by ρ_(ν).

choices.text: It can happen only when the sample is in complete darkness
choices.why: Spontaneous emission occurs whether or not light is present; its rate is simply independent of the light.

explanation: Spontaneous emission happens without outside influence, so its rate depends only on A_21 and on how many atoms are excited. Absorption and stimulated emission are driven by the light, so their rates carry a factor of ρ_(ν).

prompt: Spontaneous emission gives photons not of one exact frequency but within a narrow range of frequencies, the spectral linewidth. What does the section say causes this?

choices.text: The energy–time uncertainty principle
Stimulated emission by neighboring atoms
choices.why: Stimulated photons match the frequency of the photon that triggered them. The linewidth comes from the energy–time uncertainty principle.

choices.text: The Boltzmann distribution of the populations
choices.why: The Boltzmann distribution sets how many atoms are in each level, not the spread of frequencies. The section credits the energy–time uncertainty principle.

choices.text: Absorption of some photons by the ground state
choices.why: Absorption removes photons but doesn't spread their frequencies. The spread comes from the energy–time uncertainty principle.

explanation: Because of the energy–time uncertainty principle, the transition produces photons within a narrow range of frequencies, called the spectral linewidth, rather than at exactly ν_21.

prompt: Spontaneous emission empties the excited state at the rate −dN_2/dt = A_21 N_2. What does the same process do to the ground-state population N_1?

choices.text: Raises it at the same rate, A_21 N_2
Leaves it unchanged
choices.why: The photon carries the energy away, but the atom itself ends up in state 1, so N_1 increases at the rate A_21 N_2.

choices.text: Lowers it at the rate A_21 N_1
choices.why: Every atom that leaves state 2 by spontaneous emission lands in state 1, so N_1 goes up, by dN_1/dt = A_21 N_2.

choices.text: Raises it at twice that rate, 2A_21 N_2
choices.why: Each decay moves one atom from state 2 to state 1, so N_1 gains exactly as fast as N_2 loses: dN_1/dt = A_21 N_2.

explanation: Each spontaneous emission moves one atom from state 2 down to state 1. So N_1 rises exactly as fast as N_2 falls: dN_1/dt = A_21 N_2.

prompt: In a strong light field, each excited atom is stimulated to emit at the rate B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) = 4.0 × 10^8 s^−1, while A_21 = 2.0 × 10^7 s^−1. The total rates are B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) N_2 for stimulated emission and A_21 N_2 for spontaneous emission. How many times faster is stimulated emission?
explanation: Both rates contain N_2, so it cancels: (4.0 × 10^8 s^−1)/(2.0 × 10^7 s^−1) = 20. In this field, stimulated emission empties the upper level 20 times faster than spontaneous emission.

prompt: With all three processes at work, dN_2/dt = B_12 ρ_(ν)(ν_12) N_1 − A_21 N_2 − B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) N_2. Which process does the positive term, B_12 ρ_(ν)(ν_12) N_1, describe?

choices.text: Absorption from state 1 into state 2
Spontaneous emission, which fills state 2
choices.why: Spontaneous emission empties state 2; it is the −A_21 N_2 term. The only term that adds atoms to state 2 is absorption.

choices.text: Stimulated emission, which copies photons
choices.why: Stimulated emission is the −B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) N_2 term: it moves atoms down, out of state 2. The positive term is absorption.

choices.text: Collisions that heat the sample
choices.why: The equation has no collision terms. Its positive term, proportional to N_1, is absorption from the ground state.

explanation: Absorption is the only process that moves atoms up, so it is the only positive term in dN_2/dt. Spontaneous emission (−A_21 N_2) and stimulated emission (−B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) N_2) both move atoms down to state 1.

prompt: To relate the three Einstein coefficients, the section assumes the two levels are in thermal equilibrium. What does this assumption let it set equal to zero?

choices.text: The rates of change dN_1/dt and dN_2/dt
The population of the excited state, N_2
choices.why: At equilibrium N_2 is constant, not zero; the Boltzmann distribution fixes it. What vanishes is its rate of change.

choices.text: The spectral energy density, ρ_(ν)
choices.why: ρ_(ν) isn't zero; at equilibrium it has the blackbody value from Planck's formula. What vanishes is the net rate of change of the populations.

choices.text: The rate of spontaneous emission, A_21 N_2
choices.why: Atoms still emit spontaneously at equilibrium. The processes balance, so the net rate of change of each population is zero.

explanation: At equilibrium N_1 and N_2 are constant, so dN_1/dt = dN_2/dt = 0. All three processes still go on, but absorption exactly balances spontaneous plus stimulated emission. Solving this balance for ρ_(ν) gives a formula to compare with Planck's.

prompt: In N_2/N_1 = (g_2/g_1)exp(−hν_12/(k_B T)), what is g_2/g_1?

choices.text: The ratio of the two levels' degeneracies
The ratio of the electrons each level can hold
choices.why: Degeneracy counts states of equal energy in a level, not electrons. g_2/g_1 is the ratio of those counts for the upper and lower levels.

choices.text: The ratio of the energies of the two levels
choices.why: The energies enter through hν_12 in the exponential. g_2/g_1 is the ratio of the numbers of states in the two levels.

choices.text: The ratio of the two Einstein B coefficients
choices.why: The B coefficients don't appear in this Boltzmann expression. g_2/g_1 is the ratio of the degeneracies, the numbers of states of equal energy.

explanation: g_1 and g_2 are the degeneracies, the numbers of states of equal energy, of the lower and upper levels. A level with more states can hold a larger share of the atoms at a given energy.

prompt: At equilibrium, N_2/N_1 = (g_2/g_1)exp(−hν_12/(k_B T)). For a transition with g_1 = 1 and g_2 = 3, the Boltzmann factor exp(−hν_12/(k_B T)) is 0.010. What is N_2/N_1? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: N_2/N_1 = (3/1) × 0.010 = 0.030. The three-fold degenerate upper level holds three times as many atoms as the Boltzmann factor alone would give.

prompt: For two levels a fixed gap hν_12 apart, how does the equilibrium ratio N_2/N_1 change as the temperature rises?

choices.text: It increases
It decreases
choices.why: A higher T makes hν_12/(k_B T) smaller, so exp(−hν_12/(k_B T)) gets larger and the upper level fills.

choices.text: It stays the same
choices.why: N_2/N_1 = (g_2/g_1)exp(−hν_12/(k_B T)) contains T, so it changes as the temperature changes.

choices.text: It rises above g_2/g_1
choices.why: The exponential factor is always less than 1, so at equilibrium N_2/N_1 stays below g_2/g_1 at any temperature; it only approaches it.

explanation: In N_2/N_1 = (g_2/g_1)exp(−hν_12/(k_B T)), raising T shrinks the size of the negative exponent, so the exponential grows toward 1. The upper level fills as the temperature rises, but at equilibrium N_2/N_1 never exceeds g_2/g_1.

prompt: Why does the section bring in Planck's blackbody formula for ρ_(ν) when it relates A_21, B_12 and B_21?

choices.text: Its ρ_(ν) must equal the one from the rate balance
It gives the populations N_1 and N_2 directly
choices.why: The populations come from the Boltzmann distribution. Planck's formula gives a second expression for ρ_(ν), which must agree with the one from the rate equations.

choices.text: It shows that spontaneous emission is impossible
choices.why: Spontaneous emission is part of the balance, and A_21 appears in the result. Planck's formula is used because its ρ_(ν) must equal the ρ_(ν) found from the rates.

choices.text: It removes the need to know any Einstein coefficients
choices.why: The Einstein coefficients are what the comparison pins down: matching the two expressions for ρ_(ν) gives A_21/B_21 and g_1 B_12 = g_2 B_21.

explanation: At equilibrium, balancing the three rates gives one expression for ρ_(ν), and Planck's blackbody formula gives another. They agree only if A_21/B_21 = (8πhν_12^3)/(c^3) and g_1 B_12 = g_2 B_21, so knowing one coefficient gives the other two.

prompt: The Einstein coefficients obey A_21/B_21 = (8πhν_12^3)/(c^3). By what factor does A_21/B_21 grow when the transition frequency ν_12 is doubled?
explanation: A_21/B_21 is proportional to ν_12^3, so doubling ν_12 multiplies it by 2^3 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Spontaneous emission becomes relatively more important for high-frequency transitions.

prompt: The Einstein B coefficients obey g_1 B_12 = g_2 B_21. If the lower and upper levels have the same degeneracy, how do B_12 and B_21 compare?

choices.text: They are equal
B_21 is larger, since emission is favored
choices.why: With g_1 = g_2, the relation reduces to B_12 = B_21. Per atom, neither absorption nor stimulated emission is favored.

choices.text: B_12 is larger, since absorption is favored
choices.why: With g_1 = g_2, the relation gives B_12 = B_21: per atom, absorption and stimulated emission are equally likely.

choices.text: Their ratio depends on the temperature
choices.why: The relation g_1 B_12 = g_2 B_21 contains no temperature. The Einstein coefficients are properties of the transition.

explanation: With g_1 = g_2, g_1 B_12 = g_2 B_21 becomes B_12 = B_21. This is why, per atom, a photon is as likely to be absorbed by a ground-state atom as to stimulate emission from an excited one.

prompt: The Einstein B coefficients obey g_1 B_12 = g_2 B_21. For a transition with g_1 = 2, g_2 = 4 and B_12 = 8.0 × 10^20 m^3/(J·s^2), what is B_21, in m^3/(J·s^2)? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e20.)
explanation: B_21 = (g_1/g_2)B_12 = (2/4) × 8.0 × 10^20 = 4.0 × 10^20 m^3/(J·s^2). Knowing one Einstein coefficient and the degeneracies gives the other B coefficient.

prompt: The section writes dN_2/dt = −A_21 N_2 − B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_12)(N_2 − (g_2/g_1)N_1), and calls the term in parentheses the net upper-state population. When can optical amplification and lasing occur?

choices.text: Only when that term is positive
Only when that term is negative
choices.why: A negative net upper-state population means absorption wins and the light is weakened. Lasing needs the term to be positive.

choices.text: Only when that term is exactly zero
choices.why: Zero means absorption and stimulated emission just balance, so there is no gain. Lasing needs the term to be positive.

choices.text: Whenever the atoms are at thermal equilibrium
choices.why: At thermal equilibrium the term is negative, because the lower level is the more populated one per state. Lasing needs it to be positive.

explanation: Optical amplification and lasing can occur only when N_2 − (g_2/g_1)N_1 > 0. This condition is called a population inversion, and it needs enough energy supplied, by optical, electrical or thermal means, to put more electrons in the upper level.

prompt: A sample has an upper level with g_2 = 3 and a lower level with g_1 = 1. Its populations are N_1 = 1.0 × 10^12 cm^−3 and N_2 = 2.5 × 10^12 cm^−3. Is there a population inversion?

choices.text: No, because N_2 − 3N_1 is negative
Yes, because N_2 is larger than N_1
choices.why: With degenerate levels the test is N_2 − (g_2/g_1)N_1 > 0, not just N_2 > N_1. Here that difference is negative.

choices.text: Yes, because N_2 − 3N_1 is positive
No, because N_2 must be at least 10 times N_1
choices.why: No factor of 10 is needed. The test is N_2 − (g_2/g_1)N_1 > 0, which fails here because 2.5 × 10^12 is less than 3 × 1.0 × 10^12.

explanation: With unequal degeneracies, a population inversion means N_2 − (g_2/g_1)N_1 > 0. Here that is 2.5 × 10^12 − 3 × 1.0 × 10^12 = −5 × 10^11 cm^−3, which is negative: per state, the upper level is still less populated, even though N_2 > N_1.
